title: Value for Money Practices in Sustainable Public Infrastructure Procurement in Ghana: Strategies for Delivering Accountable, Transparent and Value-Driven Public Infrastructure
content: Purpose–Public infrastructure procurement in Ghana continues to grapple with persistent inefficiencies and weak enforcement of existing accountability framework despite the existence of the Public Procurement Act and related legal instruments. As a result, this study examines the key barriers and enablers of Value for Money (VfM) in the procurement of sustainable public infrastructure and proposes key practices for achieving VfM within the emerging regulatory landscape shaped by the Value For Money Office Act, 2026 (Act 1172). Design/methodology/approach-The study further adopted a quantitative research method by utilising survey questionnaires to collect 100 responses. The collected data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Findings and value–The findings indicate that achieving VfM in sustainable public infrastructure procurement in Ghana depends on interconnected managerial, institutional, and sustainability factors. Key barriers identified include ineffective use of VfM tools, poor contract management, corruption, inadequate risk management, weak stakeholder engagement, limited competition, political interference, and poor data management. Major enablers also include ethical and sustainable procurement, strategic planning, effective competition, performance management, technology adoption, and effective stakeholder engagement. Finally, key VfM practices identified include ethical sourcing, cost-benefit analysis, life-cycle assessment, environmental considerations, capacity building, and stakeholder engagement across procurement processes. Practical implications – In practice, the findings provide a roadmap for developing more effective and sustainable procurement policies and strategies for the quantity surveyor and procurement professional in infrastructure delivery. Originality–This study provides an integrated Ghana-specific empirical account of how barriers, enablers and sustainability-oriented VfM practices interact in public infrastructure procurement, offering evidence directly relevant to emerging VfM governance reforms. Conclusion – The study recommended strengthening training and capacity building for quantity surveyors and procurement professionals on technology adoption, ethical, and sustainable procurement practices for accountable, transparent, value-driven public infrastructure delivery.
